current_bottleneck: Pure encoded-increment modeling fixes much of the native joint anchor-factor dependence problem but loses level/state anchoring. The result is plausible joint daily changes but explosive IV level paths, invalid factor ranges, weak mean reversion, and extreme pathwise jumps over 30-day integration.
last_result_summary: 628a trained one joint38 AR transition model on encoded daily changes and reconstructed levels by integration. IV full-suite score was 3/11: conditionality, block-AR, and cross-cell passed, but surface explosion rate was 76.6%, mean-reversion ratio was -0.149, pathwise max-jump KS was 0.724, and q90/q99 jump ratios were 28.117/698.619. The joint-panel audit improved sharply: factor KS mean 0.116, 12/13 factor KS pass, q99 ratio median 1.397, 12/13 q99 pass, factor-factor corr 0.720 with generated mean abs corr 0.140 vs GT 0.225, and IV-factor corr 0.849 with generated mean abs corr 0.113 vs GT 0.149.
next_step_recommendation: Implement 629a as a unified state-conditioned increment law: generate encoded daily changes for every channel, but condition the transition on both recent encoded levels and recent encoded changes. This keeps the 628a joint-dependence gain while restoring level anchoring and mean reversion without IV/factor-specific branches or post-hoc corrections.
current_best_note: 510a/392a remain the historical short-frame best learned IV laws at 8/11. On the 441-window broad frame, 510a, 596a, and 610a all score 5/11. 574a remains the best risk-manager joint stress product but is a composed deck, not a calibrated joint law. 610a is the cleanest native joint learned law so far because it generates IV and anchor factors through one shared AR transition model.
oracle_feasibility_note: 435a reaches 11/11 only as a validation-future oracle upper bound; it is not a deployable or learned conditional scenario generator.
